opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the first thing to say is that "fast" on its own is the wrong goal. In formal verification, the solver is one part of a larger loop. A verification engineer writes a spec, the tool generates queries, and the solver answers them. What matters most is whether that whole loop stays productive for the person using it.

So I'd point to a few priorities.

The first is soundness, and it isn't negotiable. If the solver says "unsat" and that's wrong, you've told someone their system is safe when it isn't. Every optimization has to preserve correctness, and ideally you produce proofs or certificates that someone can check independently. Being fast and wrong is worse than useless.

The second is performance on the queries people actually generate, not on benchmarks. Queries from verification tools have a particular shape. They're often huge, heavy on quantifiers or bit-vectors, full of structure the frontend left behind, and highly repetitive across runs. A lot of the real gains come from understanding that distribution. Good preprocessing, exploiting incrementality so you don't re-solve the same context again and again, and picking strategies tuned to the theories that really show up. Winning a competition benchmark doesn't always mean your users' queries get faster.

The third is predictability, which people tend to underrate. Verification engineers hate instability. A tiny change to the code, or even renaming a variable, can flip a query from one second to a timeout. That kind of brittleness destroys trust and productivity. Sometimes I'd rather have a solver that is a bit slower on average but stable than one that is brilliant on some inputs and falls off a cliff on others.

The fourth is useful output when things fail. When a query comes back "sat" or "unknown", the user needs a model, a counterexample, or an unsat core that helps them work out what went wrong. Diagnostics are part of the product.

Finally, you have to think about the system as a whole. A lot of the time the biggest win isn't inside the solver at all. It's in how the verification tool encodes the problem, or in caching and parallelism across many queries. Co-designing the frontend and the solver usually beats tuning either one alone.

So my short answer is: correctness first, then the latency the user actually experiences on real workloads, with stability valued about as highly as raw speed.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The honest answer is that what matters most is usually not the thing people expect, which is raw solving speed on hard benchmarks.

When you're using an SMT solver inside a formal verification pipeline, the queries you actually see look very different from competition benchmarks. You get an enormous volume of queries, most of them are easy, and a lot of them are nearly identical to each other because they come from the same program being checked over and over with small changes. So the first thing I care about is incremental performance and predictability. If a developer changes one line and the verifier takes five minutes instead of five seconds, they stop running it. A solver that's a little slower on average but never has those cliffs is far more valuable than one that wins benchmarks and occasionally times out for no visible reason.

The second thing is the interface between the verifier and the solver. A huge fraction of performance comes from how you encode the problem: how you handle quantifiers and triggers, how you manage theory combination, whether you let the solver see structure it can exploit or whether you've flattened everything into a soup it has to rediscover. I've seen bigger wins from changing an encoding than from any solver-internal optimization.

And third, when things go wrong, the solver needs to tell you something useful. Unsat cores, good counterexample models, some way to explain why a query is slow. Verification engineers spend most of their time debugging failed proofs, not admiring successful ones, so the solver's explainability is part of its performance in a real sense.

So if I had to compress it: optimize for the workload you actually have, make the common case fast and the worst case bounded, and treat the solver as part of a system rather than a black box you benchmark in isolation.

astra-6.text:
I think the first question is: what does the formal verification application actually need from the solver? There isn’t one optimization that matters most for every workload. The kinds of formulas you generate, the theories involved, and whether you make one large query or many incremental queries all affect which improvements are useful.

Correctness is fundamental, of course. A fast answer is only valuable if you can trust it. Beyond that, I would focus on representative workloads and look at both runtime and how many problems the solver can solve within a resource budget. An improvement in average runtime can hide regressions on particularly difficult cases.

And I would look at the interaction between the verification tool and the solver. Sometimes changing the encoding, or preserving useful work across related queries, has a bigger impact than optimizing an individual solver operation. So the objective is really to make the overall verification process more effective, and use that to guide the solver optimizations.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first question is: what workloads are we optimizing for? In formal verification, improving the average runtime on a benchmark suite is useful, but it doesn’t tell the whole story. You also care about how many problems you can solve within the time and memory budget, and whether you can handle the difficult cases that block a verification task.

Then, of course, correctness is fundamental. A fast answer is only useful if you can trust it. So I would look at performance together with robustness, testing, and, where the application needs them, proofs or models that can be checked.

The other important piece is the interaction with the verification tool. How it encodes a problem, whether it uses incremental solving, and what information it asks the solver to return can all change which optimization matters. So I wouldn’t start by saying one algorithm is the most important. I would start with the actual verification workflow, identify the bottleneck, and measure whether a change helps that workflow.
